Élections : Que propose-t-on aux aînés?: Elections: What’s on offer for seniors?
La campagne électorale lancée le 15 août: The election campaign launched by Justin Trudeau on August 15 has a minimum length of 36 days, as required by law.

The election campaign launched by Justin Trudeau on August 15 has a minimum length of 36 days, as required by law. That constraint is a challenge not only for organizations like Elections Canada, which have to find staff very quickly, but also for seniors like Lucile Nadeau-Brunet. The nonagenarian recently moved to a new neighbourhood, which means she has very little time to register on the voters list if she wants to be able to vote on September 20. However, Elections Canada only allows people to register in advance on the voters list online, a service Ms. Nadeau-Brunet does not have access to.
Comme elle n’est pas en mesure de s'insc: Because she is unable to register in advance online, she has not received the documentation that tells her which polling station she should go to. To vote, she therefore has to find out on her own where her polling station is and register on voting day itself. Same-day registration comes with its share of challenges and stress for someone her age, since she has to make sure she brings all the documents the process requires.
Celle qui aura bientôt 100 ans ne cache: The woman, who will soon turn 100, makes no secret of her distress at the difficulty of completing all these steps on her own. “I hardly see anyone [because of the pandemic]. If one of my friends had said to me, ‘come on, I’ll go with you [to register on the voters list],’ I would have done it, but right now that’s not possible.”
Le Parti libéral a une promesse claire e: The Liberal Party has a clear promise when it comes to seniors’ access to services. Justin Trudeau’s team commits to creating a toll-free number to “help seniors access government support.” This line would serve as a “single point of access to a wide range of government services and benefits.”
Le Nouveau Parti démocratique (NPD) veut: The New Democratic Party (NDP), for its part, wants to help seniors access technology by increasing “funding for community programs,” without specifically mentioning a desire to simplify access to government services. The Bloc Québécois “proposes an investment of $15 million to expand financial assistance services [...] particularly for seniors, through community services.”
Cette promesse comprend de l’aide gratui: This promise includes free help with preparing tax returns, searching for benefits and budget counselling. As for the platforms of the Greens and the Conservatives, they make no mention of this issue.
« Le sujet qui parle le plus à nos membr: “The issue that resonates most with our members is seniors’ financial insecurity,” says FADOQ network president Gisèle Tassé-Goodman without hesitation.
Celle qui dirige le plus grand organisme: The head of the largest seniors’ organization in Canada, with more than half a million members, cites rising rents and the increasing cost of groceries to back up her claim. “Seniors are struggling to make ends meet,” she says. On the FADOQ website, Ms. Tassé-Goodman explains, you can see hundreds of testimonials describing the economic hardships seniors are facing.
« Ils sentent que le gouvernement n’a pa: “They feel that the government has not listened to their needs,” she laments. She is also particularly outraged by the creation of “two classes of seniors,” which stems from the announcement, in Justin Trudeau’s government’s most recent budget, of a 10% increase to Old Age Security pensions for people 75 and over. Seniors aged 65 to 75, who also receive the Old Age pension, are excluded from this boost.
Comme mentionné ci-haut, les Libéraux ve: As mentioned above, the Liberals want to “continue implementing [their] plan to increase Old Age Security (OAS) benefits by 10% next year for seniors 75 and older.” They also promise to “increase the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) by $500 for seniors living alone and $750 for couples, starting at age 65.”
Les Conservateurs veulent inciter les aî: The Conservatives want to encourage seniors to stay in the workforce by “doubling the Canada Workers Benefit up to a maximum of $2,800 for individuals and $5,000 for families.” This measure would therefore offer “a $1/hour wage increase to low-income seniors who decide to work part-time.”
Le Bloc Québécois dénonce l’augmentation: The Bloc Québécois denounces the increase in OAS solely for those 75 and over, which “represents only half of recipients.” It is calling for “a substantial $110 per month increase to the OAS pension for all seniors 65 and over.” The NDP wants to ensure that no senior has their GIS benefits suspended because of an administrative problem. That is why they want, within a year, to stop this practice against those who are unable to file their tax returns within the prescribed deadlines.
Le Parti vert offre plusieurs propositio: The Green Party offers several proposals to reduce the financial burden on seniors, such as a guaranteed livable income and pharmacare, though without giving precise figures on what these measures would amount to.
L'habitation est un cheval de bataille p: Housing is a cause close to Lucile Nadeau-Brunet’s heart; even though she is approaching 100, she still lives in her own home. She wants politicians to allow seniors to “remain masters of their own homes” and thereby give more older people the chance to grow old at home.
Pour Mme Nadeau-Brunet, les maisons des: For Ms. Nadeau-Brunet, the seniors’ residences (maisons des aînés) announced by the Legault government in the wake of the tragedy in Quebec’s CHSLDs do not represent a real change in how society handles old age. “They have to be homes that let seniors feel at home and get involved in society in their own way,” she explains. Her vision of old age is not one where seniors are excluded from society’s choices, but one where they are full participants in the decisions that affect them.
Les propositions des Conservateurs et de: The Conservatives’ and Liberals’ proposals on support for home care are fairly similar. Both parties want to increase the Home Accessibility Tax Credit, a measure that helps adapt a home to the needs of an older person with reduced mobility. The Liberals want to double this tax credit to $20,000, while the Conservatives want to raise its limit from $10,000 per dwelling to $10,000 per person.
Le parti d’Erin O’Toole veut aussi créer: Erin O’Toole’s party also wants to create the Canadian Seniors Care Benefit, which would pay $200 a month to any household that lives with and cares for a parent over 70. Echoing one of the demands made by FADOQ, the NDP, if elected, would make the caregiver tax credit refundable. The Green Party, without giving a figure, wants to provide the provinces and territories with a special seniors’ care transfer, dedicated to specific improvements to home care.”
Le Bloc Québécois, bien qu’il ne propose: The Bloc Québécois, although it does not propose specific housing measures for seniors, is asking “that 1% of the federal government’s budget be allocated to the construction of social and community housing.”
Gisèle Tassé-Goodman ne se fait pas d’id: Gisèle Tassé-Goodman has no illusions about the challenges ahead in the coming months, no matter which government is elected. “For us, the commitments made to seniors must be fulfilled, and the government must listen to older people,” she hopes. The pandemic has hurt the living conditions of the population she advocates for, and she believes that the well-being of Canada’s seniors depends on a combination of several factors, such as financial security and an effective health care system.
Elle se réjouit que six des sept priorit: She is pleased that six of the seven priorities set out by her organization have made their way into the federal parties’ platforms. And if one of her demands could be met, which would she choose?
